spatial_claims.claim: E is inside the circle; AC and BD intersect at E
Case 1: E coincides with centre F (both chords are diameters); AE=EC=DE=EB as radii
Case 2: F lies on AC (AC is a diameter); FG is perpendicular from F to BD; G is on BD; DG=GB (bisection by III.3)
F is midpoint of AC; E is on AC but not at the midpoint (unequal partition for II.5)
Triangle FGE is right-angled at G; G and E are both on BD, F is off BD
Triangle FGB is right-angled at G; G and B are both on BD, F is off BD
BD is cut equally at G and unequally at E (partition for II.5)
Case 3: Diameter through F and E is drawn; G is named as intersection of diameter with BD (but G=E since E is already on both)
Diameter FH intersects chord AC at E; Case 2 applied to give FE*EH = AE*EC
Diameter FH intersects chord BD at E; Case 2 applied to give FE*EH = DE*EB

configuration_map:
Case 1: E = F = centre. All segments AE, EC, DE, EB are radii. Trivially consistent.

Case 2: Circle with centre F. Diameter AC passes through F (midpoint of AC). Chord BD does not pass through F. The two chords intersect at E (inside circle, on AC but not at midpoint F). Perpendicular from F to BD has foot G on BD, which bisects BD. Triangles FGE and FGB are right-angled at G. G and E are distinct points on BD (G is the midpoint of BD, E is the intersection with AC). All positions are mutually consistent.

Case 3: Circle with centre F. Neither chord AC nor BD passes through F. They intersect at E inside the circle. A diameter is drawn through F and E, meeting the circle at two endpoints. Since E lies on BD and E lies on the diameter, the diameter intersects BD at E. The point G introduced as 'intersection of diameter with BD' equals E. Steps 13-15 apply Case 2 twice using the diameter and each chord, both intersecting at E. The result FE*EH serves as a common value proving AE*EC = DE*EB. All positions are consistent.
pass_reason: All spatial claims are mutually consistent across all three cases. Case 2 correctly establishes perpendicular foot G on BD as distinct from intersection point E, and applies II.5 and I.47 to valid right triangles. Case 3 has a notational issue (G is introduced as if distinct from E when G=E), but this does not affect the mathematical argument since Steps 13-15 only use E as the intersection point and correctly apply Case 2 twice via the common product FE*EH. No angle decompositions are used; the proof relies entirely on segment products and the Pythagorean theorem applied to properly configured right triangles.
